baseline.note: The first structured baseline. Every rule below is relative to this commit and states why it exists. A limit is a deliberate ceiling chosen from the product requirement, not a copy of the measured value; where no such ceiling could be justified, the rule is a tolerance on the baseline instead.

rules.reason: The reactive core. It is the base every consumer pays for, so a 15% drift is a real change in the floor, while a smaller move is optimisation noise across compilers and zlib versions.

The DOM runtime is the largest framework download for a typical app. It changes only when a runtime capability is added; 10% is roughly one medium feature. Any larger jump must be accompanied by a measurement of the consumer scenarios in docs/performance/build-size-audit.md.
The public entry point. It re-exports runtime-dom, so it moves with it; the tighter-looking tolerance is equivalent once the shared code is accounted for.
Tiny shared helpers (7.7 KiB). A 20% tolerance avoids failing on a 1.5 KiB helper while still catching a whole new module appearing.
Routing is optional but always on the critical path when used. The browser build bundles the resolver; growth there is a consumer cost.
A thin wrapper over @tanstack/query-core. The wrapper itself is 15 KiB; a 20% move means a new export surface.
4-7 KiB. Same reasoning as shared: small absolute numbers need a wider relative band to be meaningful.
The ICU runtime and its parser. Locale data is not bundled here, so the runtime itself should be stable.
Server rendering is not on the browser critical path, but it is published and its size is a deployment cost.
The compiler entry is a thin re-export; the Rust binary does the work. A large jump here means JS logic leaked into the wrapper.
Build-time only, but it is loaded by every consumer's dev server, so its install and start cost is real.
The Playground's shared bridge. @babel/parser is external to it, so the published size is the engine and not the parser.
The browser compiler. Raw bytes matter because the browser downloads the .wasm body; 15% is one dependency bump in the oxc/parser stack. A larger change must come with a wasm-opt measurement.

The seven napi platform binaries. They are installed, not downloaded by a browser, but they are the largest npm payload a consumer receives. Rust release profile changes move these by a few percent; 10% catches an accidental debug build.
Build-time analysis that also ships a browser entry used by the WebC Studio.
Build-time declaration generation.
Build-time integration for the WebC pipeline.
WebC output emitters.
Small output emitter; wider band for the same reason as shared.
Small output emitter.
Wrapper generator; its output is what a consumer ships, so a drift here multiplies.
Wrapper generator.
The WebC pipeline entry.
The WebC runtime bridge, loaded by every generated custom element.
Developer tooling; not shipped to users.
Test helpers; not shipped to users.
Shared compiler model types.
The component registry shipped to consumers of create-zeus. It is a data-plus-lookup module, so a wider band keeps registry entries from failing the build while still catching a runaway import.
The scaffolding CLI. Templates are copied rather than bundled, so the published entry is small and stable.
The companion CLI entry.

expectedUnmeasured.reason: the scaffolding CLI is built by 'pnpm -F create-zeus build', which needs its own node_modules; the package build and the size report do not build it
